3. It was the further case of the petitioner-Bank that the goods pledged would value at Tk. 3,79,500/-. In spite of demands, the company had not secured the liability and it appears that it had no capacity to adjust the liability and repay the loan with interest. The company had failed and was neglecting to pay its debts on demand and, in fact, it was unable to repay the debts. Since the company was unable to repay its debts to the petitioner-Bank, the company is liable to suffer liquidation under law. The petitioner-Bank prayed for winding up the company as it failed to pay the loan of Tk. 39,41,371.12 as stood on 14.10.82. 

 4. The company appeared before the Court, contested the aforesaid application of the petitioner-Bank and denied its liability and the allegations made in the application by filing affidavit-in-opposition. It is their case that the industrial enterprise has been taken over as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 and thereafter it was placed tinder the statutory corporation by President's Order No. 27 of 1972. It was their further case that the goods were pledged and the petitioner-Bank was in custody of those goods worth Tk. 3,79,500/- and the petitioner-Bank did not allow the company to have its goods and sell those at the appropriate time at appropriate value for liquidating its debts. Due to the fault of the petitioner-Bank, the company had to suffer loss and damage estimated at about Tk. 30,00,000/-. The market value of the raw materials held by the petitioner-Bank amounted to Tk. 3,79,500/-. It is their further cast that if the loss of Tk. 30,00,000/-is adjusted against the claim of the petitioner-Bank, the outstanding dues would remain only at a few lakh Taka. It is stated by the company that the liability as regards interest during the period from the date of taking over till the date of release are not the legal liabilities of the company and the maximum penal rate of interest should not be charged against the company. If the value of the goods pledged, the damage caused by the action of the petitioner-bank and the interests charged upon the company for the whole period of unrest and for the period it was under the corporation are taken up together and adjusted, then there will be no liability of the company to the petitioner-Bank. Since the company had counter-claim for damages for non-delivery of the goods on cash payment in time and there were disputed claims, an application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act is not maintainable. 

 7. The company filed a further affidavit-in-opposition on 19.11.86 stating that the title deeds of land measuring 13 bighas in Kashimpur mouza were deposited with Agrani Bank, Local Office, Motijheel as collateral security against loan given to the company. It was their further case that the existing value of the aforesaid 13 bighas of land would be Tk. 45 lacs approximately. In another affidavit-in-position which was filed in Court on 13.2.86 by the company, it appears that the interests during the period of turmoil in 1971 and after nationalization stood at Tk. 14,25,702/- and if the aforesaid amount of interests is deducted from the total claim, then all the liabilities stood fully secured and as such the petitioner-Bank is not entitled to go for a winding up proceeding. 

 8. During the hearing of the aforesaid matter before the Company Court, another alleged creditor, namely, Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) appeared and filed an affidavit before the Court on 10.7.85 alleging that the aforesaid company was liable to it for an amount of Tk. 59,46,131.03 and for the aforesaid amount, the BCIC had already filed Money Suit No. 40 of 1980 and Money Suit No. 244 of 1982. It is their case that on liquidation its loan should be adjusted out of the sale-proceeds of the property of the company. Against the aforesaid affidavit of BCIC, the company also filed an affidavit-in-opposition disputing its liability. 

 9. Another creditor Bangladesh Shilpa Bank also filed an affidavit before the Company Court on 17.3.83 and claimed that the company was liable to it for an amount of Tk. 72,58,914.09. It was their case that it should not be liquidated. Alternatively it prayed that if it is liquidated, then their dues being first charge should be satisfied first. The Shilpa Bank also filed a case being Miscellaneous Case No. 107 of 1979, subsequently renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 50 of 1984 iii the Commercial Court, Dhaka, claiming the above amount. Ultimately, on 28.6.86 the Shilpa Bank got a decree for Tk. 20,30,793.46. Against the aforesaid decree both the petitioner-Bank and the Company filed two miscellaneous appeals in this Court which are pending for hearing. 

 11. Before going into the merit of the appeal, let us first consider the claims of the Shilpa Bank and the BCIC. It is on record that BCIC had already filed two suits against the appellant-company and those were pending in Court at the relevant time. Since the BCIC had already gone before the Court in order to establish its claim, it is not proper for us to make any comment or say anything about it in this judgment. In the similar way, we have seen that the Shilpa Bank also filed a miscellaneous case against the appellant-company and obtained a decree as stated above, and both the parties filed two separate appeals in this Court against the aforesaid decree. So, we are reluctant to make any comment or consider about the alleged claim of the Shilpa Bank in this appeal. In order to dispose of the present appeal, we may rely and use the relevant statements of facts which have been produced before this Court by submitting affidavits by the BCIC and the Shilpa Bank. But mere reliance on such statements in this judgment will not prejudice any of the parties in their respective suits and appeals. 

 12. Dr. M Zahir, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the present application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act is not maintainable in view of the fact that there was counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/- by the appellant-company. It is his case that if the amount of Tk. 30,00,000/-, value of the goods pledged and the security given to the petitioner-bank are taken up together, in fact, there would be no liability. We are unable to accept the first contention of Dr. Zahir in view of the fact that this counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/- for damage has not been proved by any evidence on record. It is just an allegation made in the counter-affidavit and no evidence has been placed before the Court in support of such counter-claim. In this view of the matter we are unable to accept the counter-claim of Tk. 30,00,000/-. 

 14. Let us now consider the claim of the petitioner-Bank amounting to Tk. 39,41,371.12 as stood on 14.10.82. Dr. Zahir submits that the interests amounting to Tk. 14,25,702.00 in total charged against the company for the period of turmoil and for the period from the date of taking over of the company till the date of release cannot be legally charged. To allow such interest is absolutely a discretion of the Court. Petitioner-Bank is not entitled to claim such interests for such abnormal period as a matter of right. Further, during the aforesaid period the Share-holders/Directors of the company had no do-main and control over the management of the company. In a word, during that period the Share-holders/ Directors had legal disabilities over the affairs of the company and as such they should not be made bound to pay interests for such period. Although the Share-holders/Directors took over the company with all its assets and liabilities at the time of release of the company in their favour, it means legal and compulsive liability. The interests in question can not be treated as compulsive liability. Dr. Zahir tried to strengthen his above argument relying upon the case of M/s. MM Ispahani Ltd. Vs. Sonali Bank, 37 DLR (AD) 1. In the above case the question of payment of interest for the period over which the Share-holders/Directors of a taken-over company like the present one came up for consideration of their Lordships. After considering the matter in details their Lordships observed as follows: 

 "64. In principle, what appears from section 34 CPC itself is that the Court is not bound by what is provided in the contract itself, the matter of awarding interest being completely within its discretion. So, in a case involving the award of interest on any dues outstanding against the debtor, the Court is free to award interest at such rate as it may think fit. Ordinarily, that means if all that has happened to the lot of the appellant company were not there and the case would have been like any other loan transaction in normal circumstances, there would have been no objection to award interest on such principles. In the very extra-ordinary circumstances of the case without interfering with the principles enunciated by the aforesaid decisions as mentioned by the learned Counsel for the respondent Bank, we arc reluctant to award any interest at all not only from the date of filing the suit till the date of the decree but for the entire period beginning from 13.12.71 to the date of the decree. The reason being the unmerited deprivation of the appellant company to enjoy riot only his property and business rights but also utilization of the loan obtained from the Bank and the security offered against the loan by the company. It is true that the Government has ultimately returned the appellant company to its former directors but even then excepting the amount of nearly Taka one crore which the administrator deposited in the company's account in 1972, neither any sum by way of compensation nor the equivalent amount of jute stocks were returned to the company. In this view of the matter we arc reluctant to award any interest on the dues outstanding on 13.12.71 for the aforesaid period. 

 (iv) if the number of members is reduced in the case of a private company, below two or, in the case of any other company, below seven; 

 17. Section 162 stipulates that a company may be wound up if the company is "unable to pay" its debts. In the present case, the petitioner-Bank is relying upon this provision is section 162(v) of the Companies Act for winding up of the company. Now, inability clause "unable to pay" has been defined in section 163. From section 163, it appears that if demand is made and within three weeks thereafter if the company neglects to pay the sum or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor, in that case it will amount to "unable to pay" for the company. 

 18. Now, let us see whether the company is unable to pay the debts or the debts have been secured to the satisfaction of the petitioner-Bank. As we have stated above if the amount of interest and the value of the goods pledged to the petitioner-Bank are taken up together and deducted, then the liability would come to Tk. 21 lacs and odd, at the relevant time. In the further affidavit of the company filed in Court on 19.11.86, it has been stated that the title deeds of lands measuring 13 bighas in Kashimpur mouza had been deposited with Agrani Bank, Local Office, Motijheel as collateral security for the company and the value would be approximately Tk. 45 lacs. On behalf of the petitioner-Bank an affidavit was Red on 16.8.88 and in that affidavit, there was assertion that there was a talk of compromise and some terms and conditions were laid down. In one of the terms, it was stated that the appellant-company shall not sell any property of the company or its sister concern which were mortgaged with the bank till liquidation of the entire liabilities of the borrower Company with the bank. There was no denial on behalf of the petitioner-Bank that the collateral security as stated above had been given to the bank. Now, Dr. Zahir submits that if the collateral security along with the value of the lands of the company where the factory is situated and the value of the machineries were taken up together, then it appears that the debts or liabilities to the bank are fully secured, and as the debt is secured on property of the company, the application for winding up under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act cannot be maintained. We find substance in the above contention of Dr. Zahir. At the time of hearing of the case, on our query, Mr. Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, has disclosed that the factory of the company is situated at Fatullah and this company has got about eight bighas of land on which the factory is situated. Today, an application has been filed on behalf of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank stating that the machineries of the factory and the lands at Fatullah Industrial Zone had been hypothecated to the Shilpa Bank. Dr. Zahir submits that the value of the eight bighas of land in Fatullah Industrial Zone together with the value of the machineries would be about Taka several crores and arc sufficient security to the out-standing dues of the petitioner-Bank. He further submits that although the Shilpa Bank has got the first charge over the above property, even then the claim of the petitioner-Bank would be satisfied by the company's property even after satisfying the first charge of the Shilpa Bank. From the facts and circumstances as well as the materials on record, we are of the view that the outstanding dues of the petitioner-Bank, as stated above, had been sufficiently secured when the application under sections 162 and 163 of the Companies Act had been filed before the Court and for that reason no winding up of the company is, at all, warranted. 

 20. Dr. Zahir has referred to the case of Bengal Luxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. and others Vs. Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Ltd. and others, reported in AIR 1955 (Cal) 273 in order to support his contention that when a bonafide dispute over the claim is made by the company, winding up proceeding on such bonafide dispute of claim is not an appropriate legal proceeding. In that case similar question arose and a Division Bench consisting of Chakravartti CJ and SR Das Gupta J, after discussing the matter in details, observed as follows: 

 "(4) The case cited does not support the whole contention of the learned Advocate-General. As the decision was relied on as having modified the statement of law, as contained in Buckley, it will be convenient to read the statement at the present stage. It runs as follows: 

 (5) In the case cited the passage was quoted from the 11th Ed. of Buckley, pp. 356, 357 and in quoting it, the learned Master of the Rules observed that the law and practice in regard to such matters have been stated in the passage "with sufficient accuracy." 

 (7) Read in the light of that principle, the true meaning of Buckley's summary of the English decisions appears to me to be this; when a company has failed to pay a debt, but it appears that the failure occurred, not because the company was unable to pay, but because it disputed the liability on a substantial ground and there is nothing to show that if the dispute is decided against the company, it will not or will be unable to pay the debt, there is not present proof of insolvency and therefore no sufficient basis for making a winding-up order. In such a case, the winding-up Court will only sec if the grounds on which the liability is disputed are substantial and if the dispute is in that sense bonafide. If it finds the issue in favour of the company, it will ordinarily not proceed further and decide the dispute itself and determine whether or not a debt exists and has become payable. 

 In such a case, the Court will either dismiss the petition for winding-up or keep it pending till the creditor has established his claim in a regular action. The principle on which the Court will forbear from deciding the dispute and making a winding-up in case it decides it against the company, is that winding-up proceedings are not intended to be exploited as a normal alternative to the ordinary mode of debt-realisation and that it is more convenient that claims should be investigated and decided in a regular action." 

 21. The principle laid down in the aforesaid judgment, we find, has got application in the facts and circumstances of the present case inasmuch as bonafide dispute over the claim of the petitioner-Bank very much exists in the present case. 

 23. We have gone through the judgment of the learned Company Judge. From the judgment, it appears that his Lordship simply incorporated the alleged claims made by the different creditors. But, unfortunately, he has not considered in details the existing assets and liabilities of the company, the alleged interests claimed and other circumstances and materials to see as to whether the company was actually unable to repay the loan or the debts have been secured. His Lordship has found that the appellant company has no bonafide defence and the debt is not, in fact, disputed as the bank papers filed in this case show that the denial of the debt is not based on any substantial ground. We are unable to persuade our-selves to accept the. above sweeping finding of the learned Company Judge in view of our discussions made above, and as such the judgment impugned in this appeal cannot he sustained in law.
